6. The factual background set out below concerns Appeal No. 600 of 2023,
filed by Beta Wind Farm Private Limited (“BWFPL”) and the corresponding Appeal
No. 746 of 2023, filed by APSPDCL, arising from the order dated 26.09.2022 in
O.P. No. 85 of 2021. The facts in respect of other WPGs are similar except that
their capacity, date of Tariff Order, normative CUF, applicable generic tariff and
date of Impugned Orders may be different.
7. By order dated 03.05.2009, the then Andhra Pradesh Electricity Regulatory
Commission (for the unified state of Andhra Pradesh) determined a generic tariff
of ₹ 3.50 per unit for wind power projects. Guttaseema Wind Energy Private
Limited challenged that order in Appeal No. 194 of 2009. By judgment dated
03.05.2011, this Tribunal allowed the appeal and remanded the matter for
redetermination of tariff on the parameters of capital cost, return on equity, CUF
and interest on working capital.
8. Pursuant to the remand, the State Commission, by order dated 15.11.2012
in O.P. No. 13 of 2012, determined a preferential generic levelised tariff of ₹ 4.70
per unit for wind power projects entering into PPAs between 15.11.2012 and
31.03.2015. The tariff was determined on a cost-plus basis using normative
parameters including a CUF of 23% and was applicable for twenty-five years from
the Commercial Operation Date (“COD”). The order permitted dispatch of 100%

system constraints and required the parties to obtain the State Commission’s
consent to their PPAs.
9. Following APSPDCL’s request dated 12.02.2013, the State Commission, by
communication dated 14.03.2013, approved the PPA proposed to be executed
with BWFPL. The parties executed the PPA on 29.05.2013, incorporating a firm
tariff of ₹ 4.70 per unit for twenty-five years from COD. BWFPL commissioned its
50.4 MW wind power project on 27.07.2013 and commenced supply to the
distribution licensee. However, while processing the invoice for July 2017,
APSPDCL restricted payment for the period from 27.07.2016 to 27.07.2017 by
applying a CUF of 23% and treated the supply beyond that level as free of cost.
BWFPL objected, maintaining that the normative CUF was a parameter for tariff
determination and did not limit the quantum payable under the PPA.
10. APSPDCL subsequently corrected the treatment of other periods but the
disputed payment for 27.07.2016 to 27.07.2017 remained unresolved. Against
2,33,77,000 units billed, APSPDCL allegedly admitted 1,07,59,061 units, leaving
1,26,17,939 units unpaid. BWFPL has quantified the unpaid principal amount at
₹5,93,04,313.
11. BWFPL approached the State Commission in O.P. No. 85 of 2021 for
adjudication of the dispute. By the Impugned Order dated 26.09.2022, the State
Commission held that the normative CUF of 23% was to be applied over the life
of the PPA with adjustments for excess generation and shortfall. It fixed payment
at ₹ 0.50 per unit for energy generated and supplied beyond the prescribed CUF,
subject to such adjustments and directed calculation and payment or adjustment
of the amounts within two months of receipt of the order.

Issue 1: Do these appeals against the truing-up order seek to reopen

6. Respondent Nos. 3 to 6 have submitted that GRIDCO had sought and

7. The essence of submission of OERC is that “truing up” exercise can not be
done to retrospectively change the methodology or principles of tariff determination

8. We have perused OERC Tariff Regulations, 2004 carefully. These

not in accordance with the Regulations.

cannot be altered at the truing-up stage is well settled. However, its application
would depend on the nature of the issue involved and the relief sought. We shall,
therefore, examine each issue in the light of the principle laid down in BSES
Rajdhani judgement to determine whether accepting the contention of GRIDCO
would amount to a retrospective change in the methodology or principles of tariff
determination, or to reopening a tariff determination already concluded at the ARR

33. The principle that a statutory power, where no period of limitation is
prescribed, must nevertheless be exercised within a reasonable time is well
settled. In State of Gujarat v. Patel Raghav Natha, (1969) 2 SCC 187, the
Hon’ble Supreme Court held that what constitutes a reasonable time must depend
upon the facts of the case and the nature of the order under revision. Construing
the revisional power of the Commissioner under Section 211 of the Bombay Land
Revenue Code in the context of permission granted for building purposes, the
Court held that the power ought to be exercised within a few months, since the
occupant may, in reliance upon such permission granted by Collector, incur
expenditure towards commencing building operations. The Court accordingly held
that exercise of the power more than a year after the Collector’s order was belated.
This principle has been consistently reiterated in subsequent decisions of the Apex
Court.
34. Drawing a direct parallel to the regulatory regime governing PPA approvals,

necessarily align, at the very latest, with the Commercial Operation Date (COD) of

ORDER
PER HON’BLE MR. VIRENDER BHAT, JUDICIAL MEMBER
1. The Review Petitioner M/s Adani Transmission (India) Limited is
seeking review of the judgement of this Tribunal dated 8th November, 2017
passed in Appeal No. 226 of 2016. We may note that out of 41 respondents
in this Review Petition, only Respondent No. 11 has appeared through
counsel on 2nd July, 2026 who submitted that the said respondent does not
wish to file any reply to the Review Petition. On subsequent date i.e. 13th
August, 2026, when the Review Petition came out for hearing, we heard
the Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the petitioner. Learned Counsel
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
R.P. No. 3 of 2018 Page 7 of 33

appearing for Respondent No. 11 submitted that he does not wish to
advance any arguments and left it to the wisdom of this Tribunal to take a
call on the contentions raised in the petition by the petitioner.
2. We may note that for evacuation of power under the Power Purchase
Agreements of 1495 MW capacity with Uttar Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam Ltd.
(UHBVNL) and Dakshin Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam Limited (DHBVNL), the
petitioner constructed a dedicated transmission system of 500 kV Mundra
– Mohindergarh HVDC bi-pole transmission line including associated 400
kV transmission lines which could evacuate 2500 MW power. Further, the
Petitioner had sought long term access for 200 MW to Maharashtra at
Dehgam sub-station of Power Grid Corporation of India Ltd. (PGCIL). In
order to avail connectivity to Dehgam substation of PGCIL, the petitioner
built a dedicated 400 kV Mundra_Sami-Dehgam D/C transmission line as
well as 400 kV Mohindergarh-Bhiwani transmission line.
3. Thereafter, the petition filed a petition before the 1st Respondent –
Central Electricity Regulatory Commission bearing petition No.
44/TL/2012, under CERC Transmission License Regulations, 2009 for
grant of transmission license for the dedicated transmission lines along
with associated bays. In terms of the order dated 8th June, 2013 passed by
the Central Commission for the said petition, transmission license was
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
R.P. No. 3 of 2018 Page 8 of 33

granted to the petitioner in respect of these dedicated transmission lines
and transmission bays on 29th July, 2013 after following due process.
4. The petitioner, thereafter, filed petition No. 184/TT/2013 before the
Central Commission on 5th September, 2013 for determination of
transmission tariff for the following assets :-
“i. Asset-1 consisting of +/- 500 kV Mundra-Mohindergarh
HVDC bipole transmission line with associated sub-stations,
bays, electrode lines and associated 400 kV lines; and
ii. Asset-2 consisting of 400 kV D/C Mundra- Dehgam
transmission line with associated system.”
5. The petition was disposed of by the Central Commission vide order
dated 18th March, 2016 thereby reducing the tariff claimed by the petitioner
on account of date for commencement of tariff, reduction of capital cost of
AC substation tariff and reduction of loan outstanding by cumulative
depreciation till the date of license. Aggrieved by the said order of the
Commission, the petitioner had approached this Tribunal by way of the
appeal No. 226 of 2016 which was disposed of vide judgement dated 8th
November, 2017, of which review is sought in this petition. Vide the said
judgement, this Tribunal remanded the case back to the Central
Commission for allowing the date of grant of transmission licensee i.e. 29th
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
R.P. No. 3 of 2018 Page 9 of 33

July, 2013 as the date of tariff commencement for the transmission assets
of the petitioner and to determine the capital cost of the said transmission
assets including Bhiwani and Dehgam substation as on date of grant of
transmission line including the consequential reliefs to the petitioner.
6. However, this Tribunal did not disturb the findings of the Commission
in the impugned order on the following aspects :-
“i. Capital cost reduction for AC Substation Portion of the
Licensed Asset, except for Dehgam & Bhiwani substation;
ii. Reduction of loan outstanding by cumulative depreciation till
the date of grant of license which has led to reduced recovery of
interest on loan. Further, consideration of cumulative
depreciation has also resulted in perpetual disallowance of
depreciation of Rs. 204.69 Crore for Asset 1 and Rs. 101.92
Crore for Asset 2 for the Review Petitioner.”
7. The instant Review Petition is confined to the above two aspects, on
which the decision of the Central Commission was affirmed by this Tribunal
in the above noted judgement dated 8th November, 2017.
8. We have heard Learned Senior Counsel for the Review Petitioner
and have perused the judgement dated 8th November, 2017 in Appeal No.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
R.P. No. 3 of 2018 Page 10 of 33

226 of 2016 as well as written submission on record. We reiterate here that
Review Petition had not been contested by any of the respondents.
9. At the outset, we may note that Section 114 of CPC is the
substantive provision dealing with scope of review and is quoted below:-
“114. Review. —Subject as aforesaid, any person
considering himself aggrieved—
(a) by a decree or order from which an appeal is
allowed by this Code, but from which no appeal
has been preferred.
(b) by a decree or order from which no appeal is
allowed by this Code, or
(c) by a decision on a reference from a Court of
Small Causes, may apply for a review of
judgment to the Court which passed the decree
or made the order, and the Court may make such
order thereon as it thinks fit.”
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
R.P. No. 3 of 2018 Page 11 of 33

10. The grounds on which review of a judgment / order can be sought,
have been specified in Order XLVII of the CPC which are reproduced
hereinbelow: -
“1. Application for review of judgment. — (1) Any person
considering himself aggrieved—
(a) by a decree or order from which an appeal is
allowed, but from which no appeal has been
preferred,
(b) by a decree or order from which no appeal is
allowed, or
(c) by a decision on a reference from a Court
of Small Causes, and who, from the
discovery of new and important matter or
evidence which, after the exercise of due
diligence was not within his knowledge or could
not be produced by him at the time when the
decree was passed or order made, or on account
of some mistake or error apparent on the face of
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
R.P. No. 3 of 2018 Page 12 of 33

the record or for any other sufficient reason,
desires to obtain a review of the decree passed
or order made against him, may apply for a
review of judgment to the Court which passed the
decree or made the order.
(2) A party who is not appealing from a decree or
order may apply for a review of judgment
notwithstanding the pendency of an appeal by
some other party except where the ground of
such appeal is common to the applicant and the
appellant, or when, being respondent, he can
present to the Appellate Court the case on which
he applied for the review.
Explanation.—The fact that the decision on a
question of law on which the judgment of the
Court is based has been reversed or modified by
the subsequent decision of a superior Court in
any other case, shall not be a ground for the
review of such judgment.”
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
R.P. No. 3 of 2018 Page 13 of 33

(Emphasis supplied)
11. A bare reading of these relevant legal provisions would make it clear
that an application for review of a judgment / order is maintainable upon
(i) discovery of a new and important matter or evidence which, after
exercise of due diligence, was not within the knowledge of the review
applicant or could not be produced by him when the judgment / order was
passed; or (ii) on account of some mistake or error apparent on the face
of record; or (iii) for any other sufficient reason.
12. The expression “error apparent on the face of record” used in Order
XLVII Rule 1 indicates an error which is self-evident and staring in the eye.
Any error or mistake which is not self-evident and has to be deducted from
a process of reasoning cannot be said to be an error apparent on the face
of record justifying exercise of power of review. Power of review can be
exercised only where a glaring omission or a patent mistake is found in
the order under review. We may also note that the power of review can
be exercised only for correction of a patent mistake but not to substitute a
view for the reason that a review petition cannot be permitted to be an
appeal in disguise.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
R.P. No. 3 of 2018 Page 14 of 33

13. In a recent judgment dated 08.09.2025 passed in Malleeswari v. K.
Suguna and Anr. SLP (C) No. 12787 of 2025 (2025 INSC 1080) Hon'ble
Supreme Court has reiterated that court’s power to review its own previous
order is strictly limited to correcting errors apparent on the face of the
record and not to rehear or substitute a different view as if it were an
appeal. It has been held in the said judgment that the power of review is
different from appellate power and is subject to the following limitations to
maintain the finality of the judicial decisions:
“15.1 The review proceedings are not by way of an
appeal and have to be strictly confined to the
scope and ambit of Order 47 Rule 1 of CPC.
15.2 Review is not to be confused with appellate
powers, which may enable an appellate court to
correct all manner of errors committed by the
subordinate court.
15.3 In exercise of the jurisdiction under Order 47 Rule
1 of CPC, it is not permissible for an erroneous
decision to be reheard and corrected. A review
petition, it must be remembered, has a limited
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
R.P. No. 3 of 2018 Page 15 of 33

purpose and cannot be allowed to be an appeal
in disguise.
15.4 The power of review can be exercised for the
correction of a mistake, but not to substitute a
view. Such powers can be exercised within the
limits specified in the statute governing the
exercise of power.
15.5 The review court does not sit in appeal over its
own order. A rehearing of the matter is
impermissible. It constitutes an exception to the
general rule that once a judgment is signed or
pronounced, it should not be altered. Hence, it is
invoked only to prevent a miscarriage of justice or
to correct grave and palpable errors.”
14. Further, after noticing the distinction between power of review and
appellate power, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has succinctly summed up
the grounds of review as under: -
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
R.P. No. 3 of 2018 Page 16 of 33

“17.1 The ground of discovery of new and important
matter or evidence is a ground available if it is
demonstrated that, despite the exercise of due
diligence, this evidence was not within their
knowledge or could not be produced by the party
at the time, the original decree or order was
passed.
17.2 Mistake or error apparent on the face of the
record may be invoked if there is something more
than a mere error, and it must be the one which
is manifest on the face of the record. Such an
error is a patent error and not a mere wrong
decision. An error which has to be established by
a long-drawn process of reasoning on points
where there may conceivably be two opinions
can hardly be said to be an error apparent on the
face of the record.
17.3 Lastly, the phrase 'for any other sufficient reason'
means a reason that is sufficient on grounds at
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
R.P. No. 3 of 2018 Page 17 of 33

least analogous to those specified in the other
two categories.”
15. We may also note that in the words of Justice Krishna Iyer (as his
Lordship then was), “a plea of review, unless the first judicial view is
manifestly distorted, is like asking for the Moon. A forensic defeat cannot
be avenged by an invitation to have a second look, hopeful of discovery
of flows and reversal of result. A review in the counsel’s mentation cannot
repair the verdict once given. So, the law laid down must rest in peace.”
(See Ghanshyam Mishra & Sons (P) Ltd v. Edelweiss Asset
Reconstruction Co. Ltd. (2021) 9 SCC 657).
16. Now, we proceed to discuss in detail the contentions of Review
Petitioner on the issues mentioned in paragraph No. 6 herein above.
“i. Capital cost reduction for AC Substation Portion of the
Licensed Asset, except for Dehgam & Bhiwani substation;
17. Learned Counsel for the Review Petitioner submitted that this
Tribunal in the judgement dated 8th November, 2017 which is under review,
while observing that the Commission used benchmark/indicative cost as a
“prudence check” tool and relied on PGCIL deposit works as enabling
actual-cost recovery for certain sub-stations including Bhiwani & Dehgam
AC substations, the capital cost for the remaining AC substation was
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
R.P. No. 3 of 2018 Page 18 of 33

mechanically clipped to benchmarks as per benchmarking order of the
Commission dated 16th June, 2010 without undertaking any prudence
check/detailed analysis of “causes” behind the excess claimed by the
petitioner.
18. It is argued that first proviso to regulation 7(2) of 2009 Tariff
Regulations permits prudence check based on benchmark norms “to be
specified by the Commission”. It is the submissions of the Learned Counsel
that the term “Specified” means specified by Regulations and not by way
of an order. He further referred to 2nd proviso of the said Regulation 7(2)
which provides that where benchmark norms have not been specified,
prudence check may be conducted by the Commission for allowing costs.
